newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia faces oil import worries after Iraq attack.
newsitem.headline: Asia faces oil import worries after Iraq attack.

text.p: A rally in crude oil prices after U.S. missile attacks on Iraq this week has raised the prospect of a further strain on the import bills of many Asian nations.

After the first missile attack on Tuesday in retaliation against Baghdad's incursions against Kurds in northern Iraq, the price of the benchmark North Sea Brent crude surged to a post-Gulf War high of $23.50 per barrel, rising more than $1.50 in one day.
Prices showed a muted response to the second missile attack, on Wednesday, as the tension was factored into the market, traders said. Prices have since calmed to $22.00.
But even before the missile attacks, average Brent prices in the year to the end of August were more than $1.50 higher at $18.63 when compared with the year-earlier $17.07.
And the prospect of a defiant President Saddam Hussein remaining in power in Iraq is likely to underpin oil prices for years to come, traders and analysts said.
For Asian countries, that could mean continued pressure on already stretched import budgets.
Asia is the fastest-growing oil consumer in the world. By 2000, the region is expected to surpass North America as the biggest consumer, analysts said.

A.K. Arora, director of the refineries and pipelines division of Indian Oil Corp, India's sole crude importer, said: "The recent U.S attack on Iraq will definitely have an impact on us, as oil prices climb and we are importing so much oil. Our import bill will increase if prices continue to rise on the tensions."
India imports 22 million to 23 million tonnes of crude and 16 million tonnes of oil products a year at a cost of $6.5 billion and around 20 percent of the national import bill.

The petroleum ministry is assessing the longer-term implications of rising oil prices, which will affect imports and a subsidy programme run by the government to compensate importers for a domestic price ceiling on many products.
China has been burdened by growing net imports of crude and oil products since the early 1990s. Net imports of crude are running at about 19 million tonnes per year, analysts said.
An official at the China National Petroleum Corp said a sustained rise in the price could force China to cut imports.

"The cut in imports could create shortages of oil products in the domestic market and its impact would be more significant in southern China provinces, which depend more on imported oil," said the official, who asked not to be named.
Import prices for China are prohibitive above $22.00, said a source at China's key crude oil trader Unipec.
South Korea, which imported 332 million barrels of crude, mostly from the Middle East, in the first half of 1996, was watching the crude price but was not worried.
"We are closely watching the situation. But I don't expect any major change on the policies," said a senior official at the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy who asked not to be identified.

Jung Eun-mi, an analyst at the Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade, said: "It's likely to settle without developing into an all-out war, and markets are expected to regain stability soon after it is settled."
Oil executives in major producer Indonesia -- a member of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) -- said the nation might receive a short-term boost.
"We will certainly get benefits from high oil prices," said an official at state-owned oil company Pertamina.
"But I think the current rise is temporary. So we can't say what impact it will have on our budget," he said.
Indonesia expects to export 286.6 million barrels of crude oil and condensate in the year to March 1997, compared with 300.9 million the previous year.
